tracks.title: Strategic Reasoning
tracks.description: Short exercises in reading a situation before reacting to it: who is actually deciding, what their real options are, and what each side knows.

lessons.title: Who is deciding?
objectives: Identify the people whose choices affect the outcome, and the options each has.
teach: A player is anyone whose own choice changes how a situation turns out for someone. People who appear in the story but make no choice, or whose choice makes no difference to the outcome, are not players.

An action is one option a player can actually choose from. Listing a player's actions means being precise about what's really on the table for them — not what you assume, not what would be convenient, but their real menu of choices.

The first step in reading any situation strategically is building this short list: who are the players, and what can each of them actually choose? Skipping this step is the single most common way to misread a situation — crediting someone with influence they don't have, or missing someone whose choice quietly shapes the result.
This sounds mechanical, but it's exactly what's missing when a decision "feels complicated": usually it's because the real list of players and actions was never made explicit.
lessons.example: You and a co-worker, Priya, are each deciding where to get lunch today: the cafe near the office or the sandwich place two blocks over. The building's landlord has no say in where either of you eats. Players: you and Priya — your choices change what happens. Not a player: the landlord. Your actions: cafe or sandwich place. Priya's actions: cafe or sandwich place.
practicePrompts: Think of a situation from this week where you weren't sure who really had a say.
Name every person in that situation whose choice would have changed the outcome.
For one of them, list what they could actually choose between.
lessons.apply: Next time you're in a situation involving more than one person, pause and name the players and their actions before deciding anything — even if it feels obvious.
lessons.reflect: Think of a recent plan that went sideways. Was there someone you treated as a player who wasn't really one — or someone you left out who was?

lessons.title: What each person wants
objectives: Rank outcomes for each person and read the numbers that stand for those rankings.
teach: Once you know who the players are and what each can choose, the next question is what each of them wants. A preference is how a player ranks the possible outcomes, from the one they like most to the one they like least.

A payoff is a number standing in for that ranking: higher means a player likes that outcome more, lower means they like it less. The exact number rarely matters — what matters is the order it represents.

A common mistake is assuming everyone wants the same thing, or quietly using your own preferences as a stand-in for someone else's. Two people in the exact same situation can rank the same outcomes completely differently.

It's also easy to muddle whose payoff you're looking at. A payoff always belongs to one specific player — "your payoff" and "their payoff" for the same outcome are two separate numbers, and mixing them up is one of the most common strategic reading mistakes.
lessons.example: You and a friend, Noor, are choosing a film: a comedy or a drama. You'd rather watch the comedy together than the drama together, but Noor finds comedies tedious and would rather watch the drama, even alone. Same situation, same two options — different rankings for each of you.
practicePrompts: Pick a shared decision you're part of right now.
Rank the realistic outcomes the way you'd prefer them.
Now rank them the way you think the other person involved would.
lessons.apply: In your next shared decision, write down your own ranking of the outcomes before you say anything — then guess the other person's ranking before they tell you.
lessons.reflect: Where have you assumed someone's preference matched yours, and been wrong?

lessons.title: Who chooses when
objectives: Tell whether choices are made at the same time or in turn, and what each person has seen when choosing.
teach: Timing is about the order choices happen in: does everyone choose at the same moment, or does one player choose first and another respond?

Information is about what each player actually knows when they choose — specifically, whether they've seen anyone else's choice yet. Timing and information are related but not the same thing: choosing "second" only gives you an advantage if you actually get to see the earlier choice before making your own.

It's easy to assume a later-choosing player has more information, but that's not automatic. Someone can choose after another player without ever learning what that player picked — for example, if there's no way to communicate in between.

Reading timing and information correctly matters because it changes what a smart choice looks like. Choosing blind, at the same moment as someone else, calls for different reasoning than choosing with their move already visible to you.
lessons.example: You post your event's start time on a noticeboard, then leave before anyone replies. Grace reads the noticeboard the next morning and sets her own event's time after seeing yours. Timing: you chose first, Grace chose second. Information: Grace saw your choice before making hers — so going second really did give her more to work with.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent situation where two people made related choices.
Was there a real order to who chose first — or did it happen at the same time?
Did the second chooser actually see the first choice before deciding?
lessons.apply: Before your next joint decision, ask explicitly: who's choosing first, and will the other person actually see that choice before they decide?
lessons.reflect: Have you ever assumed someone had seen your choice when they hadn't — or the reverse?

lessons.title: When your result is not yours alone
objectives: Recognise when your result depends on another person’s choice, and describe a situation completely.
teach: Strategic dependence is what makes a situation genuinely strategic rather than just an ordinary decision: your result depends not only on your own choice, but on someone else's choice too.

Without strategic dependence, there's nothing to "read" about the other person — you could just pick whatever's best for you and ignore them entirely. With it, the same choice of yours can turn out well or badly depending on what they do, so sizing up the other player's likely choice stops being optional.

By this point you have every piece needed to describe a strategic situation completely: the players, each one's actions, each one's preferences, what each knows and when, and whether their choices depend on each other.
Putting all of this into words, deliberately, before reacting is the actual skill this track is building. It feels slow at first. With practice it becomes close to automatic.
lessons.example: You and a neighbour, Tom, each decide whether to put bins out early or on collection day. If you both choose early, the street looks tidy. If you choose early and Tom doesn't, your bin sits out alone looking untidy. Your best result depends on what Tom does — that's strategic dependence.
practicePrompts: Pick a situation involving someone else's choice alongside yours.
Check: does how well things go for you actually change depending on what they choose?
If yes, describe the full situation in one or two sentences: players, actions, who wants what.
lessons.apply: Pick one real situation this week with another person and write out the full description: players, actions, preferences, timing, information, and whether your outcomes depend on each other.
lessons.reflect: What's one situation where you reacted on instinct, without really asking what the other person was likely to do?

lessons.title: Reading the Whole Situation
objectives: Combine players, actions, preferences, payoff, timing, information and strategic dependence to read one situation completely, not one piece at a time.
teach: Every real situation hands you all of this at once, not one labelled piece at a time: who's actually a player, what they can choose, what they want, who knows what and when, and whether your result depends on theirs. This week's four lessons separated those pieces out to learn them cleanly. This lesson puts them back together.

Treating each question in isolation, as if the earlier lessons' topics don't interact in a single scenario. A real situation doesn't announce 'this part is about timing, this part is about preferences' — reading it means pulling out whichever pieces actually matter, together, without being told which lesson they came from.

None of this week's questions is actually new, either — putting them together is just applying the same best-response and dependence reasoning to a fuller picture at once, rather than to one isolated piece.
lessons.example: You and a neighbour, Faisal, are each deciding whether to mow a shared strip of grass this week. You post a note on the shared fence saying you'll do it Tuesday; Faisal reads it Wednesday. Faisal would rather you mow it than do it himself, but if neither of you does, it gets overgrown and bothers you both. Reading this completely: players are you and Faisal; actions are mow or don't; you chose first (timing), and Faisal saw your note before deciding (information); Faisal's top preference is you mowing it, but his actual result still depends on what you do (strategic dependence).
practicePrompts: Pick a situation you're in that involves at least one other person.
Try to name every piece at once: who's a player, what they can choose, what each wants, who knows what and when.
Check whether your result in it actually depends on what the other person chooses.
lessons.apply: Next time a situation involving someone else feels complicated, write out the full picture in one go — players, actions, preferences, timing, information, and whether your results depend on each other — rather than reasoning about pieces of it separately.
lessons.reflect: Think back over this week's four lessons. Which single piece — players, preferences, timing, or strategic dependence — do you most often skip when sizing up a situation in real life?

lessons.title: If you knew their choice
objectives: Find the action that gives you the most against a known choice of the other person, comparing within that choice.
teach: A best response is the action that gives you the highest payoff, given one specific choice by the other player. It's always a response to something — asking "what's my best response?" only makes sense once you've fixed what the other person is doing.

Finding a best response means comparing your own options against each other, for that one fixed choice of theirs — not comparing across their different choices, and not mixing in what would happen if they'd chosen differently.

A common error is comparing the wrong things: picking the action that would be great if the other player did something else, rather than the action that's actually best against what they're doing. Another is stopping halfway — checking that one of your options looks decent, without checking whether a different one of yours would do even better against that same choice.

Best response is the building block nearly everything else in this track is built from: dominance, coordination, and reasoning under uncertainty are all, underneath, repeated applications of "what's my best response to this?"
lessons.example: You and a friend are walking to meet up, through the main gate or the side gate. You find out your friend has already left for the side gate. Given that, your best response is whichever gate gives you the better result against side gate specifically — not whichever gate would be better if your friend had gone to the main gate instead.
practicePrompts: Pick a decision where someone else's choice is already fixed or known.
List your own options for responding to that specific choice.
Pick the one that does best against that one choice, not any other.
lessons.apply: Next time you know, or can reasonably guess, what someone else has already decided, explicitly work out your best response to that specific choice before acting.
lessons.reflect: When have you reacted to what you expected someone to do, rather than what they'd actually done?

lessons.title: When the better choice flips
objectives: See that your better choice can change with the other person’s choice, as when matching or differing is what pays.
teach: Sometimes your best response doesn't depend on the other player's choice at all — one of your options is simply better, whichever they pick. Other times it flips entirely: what's best for you changes depending on what they do.

When your best response flips to match theirs, that's called coordination — you both do best when you end up making the same choice. When it flips to differ from theirs, that's anti-coordination — you do best when you end up choosing differently.

Telling these apart matters because they call for opposite instincts. In coordination, the goal is converging on the same choice. In anti-coordination, deliberately matching the other player is the mistake.

The only reliable way to tell which situation you're in is to check your best response against each of the other player's choices in turn, rather than guessing from a gut feel about whether you "want the same thing."
lessons.example: You and a colleague are each picking a video call platform for a meeting you're both joining. If you pick the same one, the call works; if you pick different ones, it doesn't. Whichever platform your colleague picks, your best response is to pick that same one — a pure coordination situation.
practicePrompts: Pick two related choices you and someone else are each making.
Work out your best response if they pick option A, then if they pick option B.
Does your best response match theirs each time, or differ from it each time?
lessons.apply: In your next shared choice with someone, work out whether you're in a coordination or anti-coordination situation before you decide — don't assume.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you and someone else ended up mismatched, on purpose or by accident. Which kind of situation was it?

lessons.title: Acting on what you believe
objectives: Choose the action that does best on average under your stated belief about the other person’s choice.
teach: Often you don't actually know what the other player will choose — you only have a belief about how likely each of their options is. A belief response is the action that does best on average, given that belief.

Working it out means weighting each possible payoff by how likely you think that choice is, adding those weighted amounts up for each of your own options, and picking whichever option has the highest total. This total is often called an expected payoff.

A belief response isn't the same as a best response to a single fixed choice — it's a best response to a whole distribution of possible choices, each with its own weight. Changing the weights can change which of your actions comes out ahead, even when nothing else about the situation changes.

This matters because real situations are rarely fully certain. Most of the time you're acting on a belief, whether you say so explicitly or not — making that belief, and the comparison it leads to, explicit is what keeps the reasoning honest.
lessons.example: You think a friend will show up early with 70% likelihood, and late with 30%. Cooking a big meal pays off well if they're early and poorly if they're late; a simple meal pays off acceptably either way. Weighting each payoff by its likelihood and adding them up for each option tells you which choice actually does better on average, given that belief.
practicePrompts: Think of a choice you're facing where you don't know for certain what someone else will do.
Estimate roughly how likely each of their options feels to you.
Work out which of your own choices does better on average, given those estimates.
lessons.apply: Before your next uncertain decision involving someone else, write down your rough belief about what they'll do as a percentage, then work out which of your options does best against that belief.
lessons.reflect: Where have you acted on a hunch about someone else's likely choice without ever making the belief, or the comparison, explicit?

lessons.title: Responding, Put Together
objectives: Combine best response, coordination and belief response to choose well whether the other side's choice is known, matched, or only believed.
teach: This week built one idea in three stages: best response (react to a known choice), coordination (notice when your best response moves to match or differ from theirs), and belief response (react to a choice you don't know yet, only believe something about). Real situations don't announce which of the three you're in.

Assuming the same approach always applies. Whether you should be matching, differing, or weighing a belief depends entirely on what you actually know about the other side's choice at the moment you're deciding — known, matchable, or uncertain are three different starting points, not one.
This is the same discipline as every lesson in this track so far: name what you actually know before choosing which tool fits, rather than reaching for whichever one you used last.
lessons.example: You and a co-presenter are picking slide software for a joint talk. If you know they've already picked one, your job is a best response: match it. If you don't know yet but think they're more likely to pick one over the other, your job is a belief response: weigh the likelihoods. Same situation, different tools, depending on what you actually know when you choose.
practicePrompts: Pick a decision involving someone else's choice.
Ask: do you actually know their choice, or only have a belief about it?
Pick the matching tool — best response to a known choice, or belief response to an uncertain one.
lessons.apply: Before your next decision involving someone else, check first whether you actually know their choice or are only guessing at it — and use best response or belief response accordingly, not whichever feels more natural.
lessons.reflect: Think of a recent decision where you treated an uncertain guess about someone's choice as if it were a known fact. What would a genuine belief response have looked like instead?

lessons.title: Checking each case
objectives: Recognise a choice that gives you more against every choice of the other person, checking each case.
teach: A dominant strategy is an action that's your best response to every single choice the other player could make — not just one of them, all of them. If you have one, there's nothing more to work out: that action is simply your best move, regardless of what they do.

Finding a dominant strategy means checking every one of the other player's possible choices in turn, and confirming the same one of your actions comes out ahead against each of them. Confirming it against just one of their choices is not enough — it has to win against every one of them.

Not every situation has a dominant strategy. When one exists, though, it's the strongest, simplest kind of answer this track deals with: you don't need to guess what the other player will do, model their incentives, or work out a belief about their choice. It's just better, full stop.

The habit to build here is discipline: resist settling for "this looks better" after checking only one of the other player's choices. A real dominant strategy survives being checked against every one of them.
lessons.example: You and a colleague each decide whether to back up a shared document to the office server or keep it local only. Backing up to the server gives you a better outcome whether your colleague backs up too or not — it beats keeping it local either way. Server is your dominant strategy.
practicePrompts: Pick a choice you're facing with more than one option.
List the other player's possible choices.
Check whether one of your options beats all your others against every one of theirs.
lessons.apply: In your next decision involving someone else, deliberately check whether you have a dominant strategy before considering what they're likely to do.
lessons.reflect: Have you ever settled on a choice after checking it against only one scenario, when you should have checked it against all of them?

lessons.title: When only one side has a sure choice
objectives: Use the other person’s sure choice to predict them, then respond to that prediction.
teach: A dominant strategy doesn't have to exist for both players at once. Often only one side has one — and when that's true, it tells you something useful about the other side, even without knowing their preferences in detail.

If the other player has a dominant strategy, you can expect them to use it: it's their best move whatever you do, so a rational player in their position plays it. That prediction is reliable in a way a guess usually isn't.

Once you can predict their choice this confidently, your own problem collapses into something simpler: find your best response to that one specific, predictable choice — exactly the skill from "If you knew their choice."

This combination — spot their dominant strategy, predict their move, then best-respond to it — is one of the most reliable patterns in reading a strategic situation, because it doesn't require guessing at all once their dominant strategy is confirmed.
lessons.example: A street vendor, Carlos, always does better selling by the market square than by the park, whichever route you take to buy from him. You can expect Carlos at the market square — not because you're guessing, but because it's dominant for him. Knowing that, you can plan your own route as a best response to a choice you can actually predict.
practicePrompts: Pick a situation where someone else's incentives are clear to you.
Check whether they have a dominant strategy.
If they do, work out your best response to that predictable choice.
lessons.apply: Next time you're unsure what to do because you're unsure what someone else will do, check first whether they actually have a dominant strategy — if they do, you don't need to guess.
lessons.reflect: Think of someone whose choice in a given situation you can predict with real confidence. What makes that choice dominant for them?

lessons.title: Choices that never pay
objectives: Tell apart situations with and without a choice that is better in every case, and spot a choice that is never better.
teach: An action is dominated when a different action gives you a higher payoff whatever the other player does — the mirror image of a dominant strategy, but describing an option to rule out rather than one to pick.
A dominated action is never your best response to anything. There's no possible choice by the other player that makes it the right move, so keeping it on the table only adds noise to your thinking.

Spotting a dominated action doesn't require knowing what the other player will actually do — exactly like a dominant strategy, it has to hold against every one of their possible choices, which is what makes it useful before you've worked out anything else about the situation.
Ruling dominated actions out early is a genuine shortcut: once you've set one aside, you never need to reconsider it, no matter what you learn later about what the other player is likely to do.
lessons.example: In a simple grid where you pick a row and the other side picks a column, suppose the other side's "Right" column always gives them less than their "Centre" column, no matter which row you pick. "Right" is dominated for them — ruled out, regardless of anything you do.
practicePrompts: Pick a decision with more than two options.
For each option, check whether some other option beats it against every possibility.
Cross out any option that's dominated this way.
lessons.apply: Before your next multi-option decision, scan for any option that's beaten by another one of your options no matter what — and rule it out immediately.
lessons.reflect: Have you ever kept an option "on the table" that, on reflection, was never actually going to be your best choice?

lessons.title: Set aside, then look again
objectives: Remove never-better choices one round at a time and check again what is left.
teach: Iterated elimination of dominated strategies (IESDS) is what happens when you don't stop at removing one dominated action — you remove it, then check what's left, because removing one option can turn a previously-fine action into a newly dominated one.

The process is: find a dominated action, set it aside, then re-examine the remaining choices as if the eliminated one never existed. Repeat. Each round can only be checked honestly against what's actually still on the table, not against options already ruled out.
This matters because dominance can be hidden by an option that will clearly never be chosen anyway. Once that option is gone, a comparison that used to look close can resolve cleanly.
The habit this builds is patience: resist declaring you're "stuck" after one round. A choice that doesn't look dominated yet might become dominated the moment something else is removed.
lessons.example: In the grid from the last lesson, once the other side's "Right" column is set aside as dominated, re-compare "Left" and "Centre" using only the rows and columns still in play. A comparison that was unclear with all three columns present can become obvious with only two left.
practicePrompts: Take a decision with several options for each side.
Remove one dominated option, for either side.
Re-check the remaining options as if the removed one never existed.
lessons.apply: Next time a multi-option situation looks tangled, remove the clearly-dominated option first and re-look at what's left before trying to solve the whole thing at once.
lessons.reflect: Where has removing one obviously-bad option from consideration made the rest of a decision easier to see clearly?

lessons.title: A tie in one case
objectives: Distinguish never worse and sometimes better from better in every case.
teach: Strict dominance requires an action to be strictly better against every one of the other player's choices — no ties allowed. Weak dominance relaxes that: an action weakly dominates another when it's never worse, and strictly better in at least one case.

The difference matters because a weakly dominant action isn't quite as safe a bet as a strictly dominant one. There's at least one scenario where it only ties rather than wins, so the case for choosing it, while still solid, is a notch less airtight.

A common mistake is treating "never worse, sometimes better" as if it were the same guarantee as "always strictly better." It isn't — confusing the two overstates how much a weakly dominant action actually has going for it.

Weak dominance still gives you a real, useful comparison: all else equal, an action that's never worse and sometimes better is a reasonable one to prefer, even without the ironclad certainty strict dominance provides.
lessons.example: A shop can join a price-match scheme or stay out of it. Joining is never worse than staying out, whatever a rival does — and strictly better if the rival runs a sale. Joining weakly dominates staying out: safe to prefer, even though there's one case, no rival sale, where it only ties rather than wins outright.
practicePrompts: Compare two of your own options across every possible choice by the other side.
Check: is one of them never worse than the other?
Check further: is it strictly better in at least one case?
lessons.apply: Next time you're comparing two close options, check specifically whether one weakly dominates the other — never worse, and better in at least one real scenario — rather than just going with a gut preference.
lessons.reflect: Where have you mistaken "never worse, sometimes better" for an ironclad guarantee, when it was really just a reasonable edge?

lessons.title: Dominance, Start to Finish
objectives: Combine dominant strategy, dominated action, iterated elimination and weak dominance into one process for narrowing down choices.
teach: This week's four ideas are really one process in stages: find a dominant strategy if one exists; notice that whatever's dominant for you makes the alternative dominated; remove dominated options and re-check what's left (iteration); and when nothing is strictly dominant, check for the weaker claim of weak dominance instead.

Treating these as four separate topics to apply one at a time rather than one narrowing-down process. In practice you check for a dominant strategy, and if none exists outright, you look for what can be eliminated, re-check, and only fall back to weak dominance once strict dominance has been ruled out.

Each stage still rests on the same single comparison from the start of this module — is one option better against every one of the other side's choices — just applied with more patience and in the right order.
lessons.example: A shop is picking a pricing tier. Checking each tier against every rival price (dominant strategy), the shop finds one tier beats all others outright — which also means the others were dominated. If no single tier had dominated outright, the next move would have been eliminating any clearly worse tier first (iteration), then checking the remainder for at least a weak-dominance edge.
practicePrompts: Pick a decision with more than two options.
Check first for a dominant strategy among your options.
If none exists, check whether anything can be eliminated as dominated, then re-check what's left.
lessons.apply: Next time you're facing more than two options, work through the narrowing-down process in order: check for a dominant strategy, eliminate anything dominated and re-check, then fall back to weak dominance only if nothing strictly dominates.
lessons.reflect: Think of a choice with several options where you picked one without really ruling the others out. Would checking for dominance, then elimination, have changed which one you picked?

lessons.title: A Stable Pair of Choices
objectives: Recognise a pair of choices where neither side's own action is a best response to switch away from, given the other's choice.
teach: A pair of choices, one for each player, is an equilibrium when each player's choice is a best response to the other's. Neither side, seeing exactly what the other picked, would want to switch to something else.

Treating an equilibrium as the best possible outcome for both players. It isn't — it only means neither side wants to unilaterally change their own choice, given what the other is doing. A pair can be an equilibrium and still be worse for both players than some other pair they aren't at.

Checking for an equilibrium means asking the best-response question twice: is your choice a best response to theirs, and is theirs a best response to yours? Both have to hold at once — confirming only one side's best response isn't enough.
This is just an application of best response, not a new kind of reasoning: an equilibrium is simply a pair of choices where the best-response check passes in both directions simultaneously.
lessons.example: You and a colleague each decide whether to back up a shared document to the office server. Server is your best response to Server, and Server is your colleague's best response to Server too — both backing up to the server is an equilibrium. Neither of you, seeing the other's choice, would want to switch to keeping it local only.
practicePrompts: Pick a situation with a pair of choices, one for each side.
Check: is your choice a best response to theirs?
Check the other direction too: is their choice a best response to yours?
lessons.apply: In your next shared decision, check both directions — is your choice a best response to theirs, and is theirs a best response to yours — before assuming you've settled on something stable.
lessons.reflect: Think of an arrangement with someone else that's lasted a while. Is it stable because neither of you wants to switch, given what the other does — or for some other reason?

lessons.title: More Than One Stable Point
objectives: Recognise when a situation has more than one equilibrium, and that nothing inside the situation itself picks one over another.
teach: Some situations have more than one pair of choices that's an equilibrium. A pure coordination situation, where both sides do best by matching each other, is a common example: both choosing option A is stable, and so, separately, is both choosing option B.

Checking only one candidate pair and stopping once it passes the equilibrium test. A situation can have a second, equally real equilibrium sitting right alongside the first one — finding one doesn't rule out another.

When more than one equilibrium exists, nothing in the payoffs themselves says which one the players will actually land on. Something outside the situation — past practice, a prior agreement, which option is more visible or familiar — is usually what settles it in practice.

Assuming that because a situation has multiple equilibria, any pair of choices at all is just as stable as any other. Most pairs still fail the equilibrium test; it's specifically the handful that pass it that are the candidates, and a real situation can have exactly one, several, or occasionally none.
lessons.example: You and a colleague are each picking a video call platform for a meeting you're both joining. If you pick the same one, the call works; if you pick different ones, it doesn't. Both picking Platform A is an equilibrium — and, separately, both picking Platform B is too. Nothing in the situation itself says which one you'll end up on; habit or a quick message beforehand usually settles it.
practicePrompts: Think of a coordination situation with more than one way to successfully match.
Check whether a second pair of matching choices is also stable, not just the first one you thought of.
Ask what, outside the payoffs themselves, is likely to settle which one actually happens.
lessons.apply: In your next coordination situation, check for a second possible stable match before assuming the first one you thought of is the only option.
lessons.reflect: Think of a shared habit or convention you and someone else settled into. Was there a real alternative that would have worked just as well, if you'd landed on it instead?

lessons.title: When Today Affects Tomorrow
objectives: Recognise when a choice is shaped by its effect on future rounds, not just the immediate payoff.
teach: Everything so far has reasoned about a single round: one choice, one payoff, done. When the same players expect to face each other again, a choice made today can also shape what the other player expects and does in future rounds — sometimes called the shadow of the future.
Reasoning about a choice as if this were the only round, when really it's one of many. What looks best for this round alone can be a poor choice once its effect on every future round is counted too.

Repetition can make a choice worth making even when it wouldn't pay off in a single round by itself — for instance, choosing not to take a one-round advantage, in order to keep an arrangement going that pays off repeatedly over many future rounds.

Assuming that repetition automatically fixes every incentive problem. It doesn't — it only matters if both sides actually expect to interact again, and know roughly how many future rounds there might be. A last round, with no round after it to protect, can reason exactly like a one-off.
lessons.example: You and a neighbour share a tool shed. Taking the last of the shared nails without replacing them would be your best move in a single interaction. But you share the shed every month — taking them without replacing them risks your neighbour stocking separately next time and no longer sharing with you at all. Replacing them protects an arrangement worth more over many future months than the nails are worth once.
practicePrompts: Think of a choice involving someone you expect to interact with again.
Ask what would be best if this were a one-off, with no future rounds at all.
Ask whether that answer changes once you count its effect on future rounds.
lessons.apply: Before a choice involving someone you'll interact with again, ask explicitly whether you're reasoning about just this round, or about its effect on every round after it too.
lessons.reflect: Where have you made a choice that only makes sense once you count its effect on a relationship or arrangement going forward, not just this one instance?

lessons.title: Starting Well, Then Mirroring
objectives: Describe a reciprocal strategy: start cooperatively, then mirror whatever the other side did last round.
Distinguish reciprocity from unconditional cooperation.
Describe a repeated situation completely, using everything covered across all four modules.
teach: A reciprocal strategy, sometimes called tit-for-tat, is simple: start by cooperating, and on every later round, do whatever the other side did on the round before. It rewards cooperation with more cooperation and answers a defection with a defection of its own.

Treating reciprocity as the same thing as always cooperating regardless of what the other side does. It isn't — a reciprocal strategy answers defection with defection just as readily as it answers cooperation with cooperation. Unconditional cooperation has no response to being taken advantage of; reciprocity does.

Reciprocity is forgiving: a single defection is met with a single defection back, not a permanent switch to defecting forever. If the other side returns to cooperating, a reciprocal strategy returns to cooperating too, on the very next round.

This is why reciprocity tends to work well in a genuinely repeated interaction: it's simple to recognise, it rewards cooperation without being exploitable, and it doesn't hold a grudge past what the other side's own behaviour currently calls for.
lessons.example: You and a colleague alternate covering each other's shifts. You cover for them whenever they ask (starting cooperatively). The one time they decline to cover for you, you decline their next request too (mirroring the defection). The time after that, they cover for you again, so you go back to covering for them too (forgiving, not holding a grudge).
practicePrompts: Think of a repeated arrangement with someone where favours or effort go both ways.
Check: do you start cooperatively, by default?
Check: if they didn't reciprocate once, did you mirror that just for the one round, or longer?
lessons.apply: In your next repeated arrangement with someone, try reciprocity deliberately: start cooperatively, mirror exactly what they did last time, and return to cooperating the moment they do.
lessons.reflect: Think of a repeated relationship where you held a grudge longer than one round after a single let-down. What would have been different if you'd mirrored just that one round, then returned to cooperating?

lessons.title: A Repeated Situation, Fully Read
objectives: Combine equilibrium, multiple equilibria, repeated interaction and reciprocity to read an ongoing relationship completely.
teach: This week asked what's stable (equilibrium), whether more than one stable point exists (multiple equilibria), what changes when the same players meet repeatedly (repeated interaction), and a simple strategy built for exactly that setting (reciprocity). Together, they're how you read an ongoing relationship or arrangement, not just a single round.

Treating an ongoing relationship as a one-off decision each time, rather than checking whether it's settled into a stable pattern, whether a different stable pattern was possible, and what today's choice does to tomorrow's.

As with every module before this one, none of these four ideas requires new reasoning — equilibrium is best response checked twice, and reciprocity is best response applied one round at a time, now with a memory of what just happened.
lessons.example: You and a neighbour have settled into always helping move each other's bins out on collection day (an equilibrium, and quite possibly one of several that could have worked). You keep doing it because the arrangement is ongoing, not a one-off (repeated interaction), and if your neighbour ever skipped a turn, you'd mirror it once rather than holding a permanent grudge (reciprocity).
practicePrompts: Think of an ongoing arrangement you have with someone else.
Check whether it's an equilibrium — would either of you want to unilaterally switch, given what the other does?
Ask whether you're treating it like a repeated relationship or reasoning about just today.
lessons.apply: Pick one ongoing arrangement in your life and read it completely: is it stable, could a different stable pattern have worked just as well, and are you reasoning about its effect on future rounds or just this one?
lessons.reflect: Across this whole module, which idea — equilibrium, multiple equilibria, repeated interaction, or reciprocity — changed how you think about an ongoing relationship the most?

lessons.title: Your Best Alternative
objectives: Identify your BATNA — what you'll actually do if this negotiation doesn't result in a deal — before negotiating.
teach: Your BATNA — Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — is what you'll actually do if this negotiation falls through. It's not a wish; it's your real fallback: another job offer, another buyer, doing the work yourself, or simply walking away.

Negotiating without working out your BATNA first. Without it, there's no way to judge whether an offer is actually good for you — you're reacting to how the offer feels, not comparing it to what you'd get anyway if you said no.

A strong BATNA is leverage, even if you never mention it directly: knowing you have a real, acceptable alternative changes how willing you are to walk away, and that willingness shapes the whole negotiation, often without a word being said about it.
lessons.example: You're negotiating a freelance rate with a client. Your BATNA is a different, slightly less exciting project another client already offered you at a known rate. That number — not a vague sense of what feels fair — is what tells you whether this client's offer is actually worth accepting.
practicePrompts: Think of a negotiation you're facing or recently had.
Name your actual fallback if no deal happens — not a hope, a real alternative.
Ask whether you'd worked that out before you started negotiating, or only during it.
lessons.apply: Before your next negotiation of any kind, write down your actual BATNA — what you'll really do if it falls through — before you say a single word to the other side.
lessons.reflect: Think of a past negotiation where you accepted a deal without really knowing your alternative. Looking back, was it actually better than what you'd have gotten anyway?

lessons.title: Your Actual Walk-Away Price
objectives: Derive a reservation value from your BATNA, and distinguish it from your target or hoped-for outcome.
teach: Your reservation value is the specific point in this negotiation — a price, a date, a set of terms — below which you're actually better off taking your BATNA instead. It's derived directly from your BATNA, translated into the terms of this particular deal.

Confusing your reservation value with your target. Your target is what you're hoping for — ambitious, aspirational. Your reservation value is the much more modest line you won't go below. Treating them as the same number means either giving up too easily or holding out for something your BATNA doesn't actually justify.

Knowing your reservation value in advance protects you from a classic trap: accepting a deal in the moment, caught up in the back-and-forth, that's actually worse than just walking away would have been.
lessons.example: Your BATNA for selling a used car is a guaranteed $4,000 trade-in at a dealership. Your target for a private sale might be $5,500. Your reservation value — the real floor — is something like $4,200, just above your BATNA to make the extra hassle of a private sale worth it. Anything below that, the dealership trade-in is simply better.
practicePrompts: Take a negotiation where you know your BATNA.
Translate it into a specific number or set of terms for this deal — your reservation value.
Check: is that the same number as what you're hoping for, or genuinely lower?
lessons.apply: Before your next negotiation, write your reservation value down separately from your target, so the two don't blur together once the conversation starts.
lessons.reflect: Where have you let your target and your reservation value blur into the same number, and how did that affect what you accepted?

lessons.title: Where a Deal Is Possible
objectives: Check whether a zone of possible agreement exists between your reservation value and theirs, rather than assuming one does.
teach: A zone of possible agreement (ZOPA) is the range between the two sides' reservation values where a deal that both would accept actually exists. If your reservation value is $4,200 and theirs (the most they'd pay) is $5,000, the ZOPA is $4,200-$5,000 — any price in that range beats both sides' alternatives.

Assuming a ZOPA exists without checking. If your reservation value is $4,200 and the most the other side would ever pay is $3,800, there's no ZOPA at all — no deal can beat both sides' alternatives, and continuing to negotiate as if one exists just wastes effort.

You usually can't know the other side's reservation value directly — it has to be estimated from what they say, what they do, and what you know about their own alternatives. Treating your estimate as certain is its own risk, but having none at all means negotiating blind.
lessons.example: You're negotiating rent with a prospective landlord. Your reservation value (the most you'd pay rather than keep looking) is $1,800. If the landlord's reservation value (the least they'd accept rather than leave it vacant another month) is $1,600, the ZOPA is $1,600-$1,800 — a real range where a deal benefits you both.
practicePrompts: Take a negotiation where you know your own reservation value.
Estimate the other side's reservation value as best you can from what you know.
Check whether a real range exists between the two — and if it doesn't, what that actually means for continuing.
lessons.apply: In your next negotiation, try to estimate the other side's reservation value early, even roughly, so you know whether you're negotiating over a real range or chasing a deal that can't exist.
lessons.reflect: Think of a negotiation that dragged on without resolving. Looking back, is it possible there was no real ZOPA at all?

lessons.title: What They Want vs What They're Asking For
objectives: Distinguish a stated position from the underlying interest behind it, to find solutions a rigid position would miss.
teach: A position is what someone is asking for in words: 'I need the deadline moved to Friday.' An interest is the actual want behind it: maybe it's not Friday specifically, but not wanting to work the weekend. Two people can hold rigid, opposed positions while having interests that are easy to satisfy together.

Treating a stated position as if it were the actual interest. Arguing over the position itself — Friday versus Monday — can block a solution that would satisfy the real interest in a way neither side had proposed, like splitting the remaining work differently.

Asking why someone wants what they're asking for, directly and without assuming you already know, is usually the fastest way to uncover the interest behind a position — faster than guessing or than holding your own ground and hoping theirs gives way.
lessons.example: A colleague insists a project must launch by Friday (their position). Asking why reveals the real interest: they're presenting it to their manager Monday morning and need it done before then. Launching Saturday evening instead of Friday satisfies that interest just as well, even though it isn't the position they stated.
practicePrompts: Think of a disagreement where someone held a firm position.
Ask yourself what interest might be behind that position, not just the position itself.
Consider whether a different solution could satisfy that interest without matching their stated position exactly.
lessons.apply: Next time someone states a firm position in a negotiation or disagreement, ask directly what's driving it, before arguing with the position itself.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you stated a firm position yourself. What was the actual interest behind it, and would a different solution have satisfied you just as well?

lessons.title: Before You Sit Down
objectives: Combine BATNA, reservation value, ZOPA and interests-vs-positions into one preparation routine before any negotiation.
teach: This week built the preparation that should happen before any negotiation starts: know your BATNA, translate it into a reservation value, estimate whether a ZOPA exists, and separate the other side's stated position from their real interest.

Walking into a negotiation having done only one or two of these, and treating that as enough preparation. Each piece covers a different blind spot — skipping any one of them leaves you negotiating on partial information, even if you feel ready.

None of this requires revealing anything to the other side. All four are things you work out for yourself, before and during the conversation, to negotiate from a clearer position — not scripts for what to say.
lessons.example: Before negotiating a salary, you'd work out your BATNA (a real other offer, or staying put), your reservation value (the minimum that beats it), an estimate of the employer's likely range (ZOPA), and the interest behind their stated budget constraint (is it really fixed, or could a signing bonus or title change the shape of the deal?).
practicePrompts: Pick an upcoming negotiation, real or likely.
Work through all four questions for it: BATNA, reservation value, likely ZOPA, their interest behind their likely position.
Notice which of the four you'd normally have skipped.
lessons.apply: Before your next real negotiation, go through all four preparation steps in writing, not just in your head, before the conversation starts.
lessons.reflect: Across this week, which of the four ideas — BATNA, reservation value, ZOPA, or interests vs positions — was most missing from how you've prepared for negotiations in the past?

lessons.title: Splitting the Pie or Growing It
objectives: Distinguish distributive negotiation (claiming a fixed amount) from integrative negotiation (creating more to share).
teach: Distributive negotiation splits a fixed amount — what one side gains, the other loses. Integrative negotiation looks for ways to grow what's available first, so both sides can end up with more than a straight split would give them.

Assuming every negotiation is purely distributive. Many negotiations have more than one issue, or differing priorities, which opens room to create value — missing that turns a negotiation that could have grown the pie into an unnecessarily tense fight over slices of a smaller one.

A single negotiation is often both: some parts genuinely are fixed and must be split, while other parts have real room to create more value first. Treating the whole thing as one mode or the other misses what's actually true about each part.
lessons.example: Negotiating a used car's price is mostly distributive — one number, fixed total. Negotiating a job offer is often integrative — salary, start date, remote days and title can all move independently, and a flexible start date might cost the employer little while being worth a lot to you.
practicePrompts: Think of an upcoming or recent negotiation.
List everything actually being decided, not just the headline number.
For each one, ask whether it's genuinely fixed (distributive) or has room to create value (integrative).
lessons.apply: Before your next negotiation, list every issue involved, not just the main one, and check each for room to create value before assuming it's a fixed split.
lessons.reflect: Think of a negotiation you treated as purely distributive. Looking back, was there a second issue that could have grown what was available?

lessons.title: Who Should Make the First Offer
objectives: Recognise how a first offer anchors the eventual outcome, and decide deliberately whether to anchor first.
teach: The first offer in a negotiation tends to anchor everything that follows — later offers and the eventual settlement cluster around it more than people realise, even when both sides know anchoring is a real effect.
Defaulting to let the other side make the first offer, out of politeness or uncertainty, without weighing that doing so usually shifts the outcome toward their anchor rather than yours.

Anchoring works best with a number you can justify if asked — an unsupported, wildly aggressive anchor can backfire by signalling you're not negotiating in good faith, undermining the very anchor you were trying to set.
lessons.example: In a salary negotiation, whichever side names a number first tends to pull the final offer toward it — a candidate who opens with a well-justified, ambitious number, backed by market research, usually ends up higher than one who waits for the employer to name a figure first.
practicePrompts: Think of a negotiation where you let the other side make the first offer.
Consider what might have changed if you'd anchored first with a justified number instead.
Think of one where you anchored first — did you have a justification ready if asked?
lessons.apply: Before your next negotiation, decide deliberately whether to make the first offer, with a justified number ready, rather than defaulting to waiting.
lessons.reflect: Where has letting the other side anchor first worked against you, in hindsight?

lessons.title: What a Concession Says
objectives: Read what the size and pace of a concession signals, without over-reading it as more than it is.
teach: A concession — giving ground on price, terms, or timing — sends a signal beyond its immediate content: how large it is and how quickly it comes both suggest something about how much room the other side still has, or how much that issue actually matters to them.

Reading a concession as revealing only one thing when several explanations fit. A quick, large concession might signal desperation — or it might just mean that particular issue was never a priority for them, and giving it up cost them little.

Concessions that shrink in size as a negotiation goes on usually signal approaching a real limit; concessions that stay large and frequent usually signal there's still plenty of room left. Watching the pattern across several concessions tells you more than reading any single one in isolation.
lessons.example: A seller drops their price by $500 in the first round without hesitation, then by $100 in the next, then refuses to move further. The shrinking pattern — not the first concession alone — is what signals they're approaching their actual reservation value.
practicePrompts: Think of a negotiation with several rounds of back-and-forth.
Look at the pattern of concessions made, not just one of them in isolation.
Consider what explanation besides 'weakness' could fit a quick early concession.
lessons.apply: In your next multi-round negotiation, track the size and pace of concessions on both sides across the whole conversation, not just react to each one individually.
lessons.reflect: Where have you read a single concession as revealing more than it actually did?

lessons.title: Trading Across What You Value Differently
objectives: Find efficient trades across multiple issues that each side values differently, rather than negotiating one issue at a time.
teach: When a negotiation has more than one issue, and the two sides don't value those issues identically, trading across them can leave both sides better off than settling each issue separately. Giving up something you care little about in exchange for something you care a lot about, where the other side's priorities are reversed, creates value neither a single-issue negotiation nor an even split would find.

Negotiating one issue fully before moving to the next. Settling price before discussing timeline, for instance, can lock in a worse deal than negotiating both together would have, once it turns out the other side cared much more about timeline than price.
Finding these trades requires knowing, or asking about, which issues matter most to each side — which is exactly what distinguishing positions from interests, from earlier this module, is for.
lessons.example: A freelancer and a client are negotiating rate and deadline together. The freelancer cares more about rate than deadline; the client, facing a tight budget but a flexible launch date, cares more about the reverse. Trading a slightly lower rate for a later deadline leaves both better off than negotiating rate and deadline as two separate, unrelated fights.
practicePrompts: Think of a negotiation involving more than one issue.
Rank how much each issue matters to you.
Consider what the other side might value differently, and what trade could follow from that.
lessons.apply: In your next multi-issue negotiation, put all the issues on the table together and look for trades across them, rather than resolving them one at a time.
lessons.reflect: Think of a negotiation you handled one issue at a time. What trade might multi-issue bargaining have revealed?

lessons.title: At the Table
objectives: Combine distributive/integrative framing, anchoring, concession-reading and multi-issue trades into one live negotiation.
teach: Last week was preparation; this week is what happens once the conversation starts. Whether to anchor, how to read concessions, and where to look for multi-issue trades all depend on first recognising whether you're splitting a fixed amount or growing what's available.

Applying one of these tools out of context — anchoring aggressively in a situation that's actually integrative, where a collaborative opening would find more value than a combative one, or missing a multi-issue trade because the conversation never widened past the first distributive issue raised.

All four build on last week's preparation: you can't anchor with a justified number without knowing your BATNA, and you can't spot a multi-issue trade without having already separated positions from interests.
lessons.example: In a salary negotiation, recognising that salary itself is somewhat distributive but title, start date and remote days are more integrative changes the whole approach: anchor firmly on salary with a justified number, but stay open and exploratory on the other issues, watching for trades the employer's own concessions reveal.
practicePrompts: Think through a negotiation you're preparing for.
Decide which parts are distributive and which are integrative before you start.
Plan whether to anchor, and what multi-issue trade you might propose.
lessons.apply: Walk into your next real negotiation having explicitly decided, in advance, which issues are distributive, which are integrative, whether you'll anchor, and what trade you might propose.
lessons.reflect: Across this week, which single tool — anchoring, concession-reading, or multi-issue trading — do you most need to practise deliberately rather than doing by instinct?

lessons.title: More Than Two People in the Room
objectives: Recognise how a third party changes a negotiation — coalitions, sequencing, and whose interests actually need satisfying.
teach: Everything so far assumed two sides. With three or more parties, new things matter: who talks to whom first, whether two parties might team up against a third, and whether a deal needs everyone's agreement or just a majority.

Reasoning about a multi-party situation as if it were still two-sided — treating one other party as THE other side while ignoring that a third party's interests, and their relationship to the first two, change what deals are actually available.

In a multi-party negotiation, the order you talk to people in can matter as much as what you say — reaching an early understanding with one party can shift what's achievable with the others, for better or worse.
lessons.example: Three roommates are splitting a renovation cost unevenly, based on room size. Negotiating with each roommate separately, one at a time, risks each one comparing notes afterward and feeling shortchanged relative to what the others got — unlike a two-person negotiation, what's fair here depends on how all three outcomes compare to each other, not just each deal in isolation.
practicePrompts: Think of a decision involving three or more people.
Consider whether any two of them might have aligned interests against the third.
Think about whether the order you'd talk to each of them in matters.
lessons.apply: Before your next decision involving three or more people, map out each person's interests separately, and consider who to talk to first and why.
lessons.reflect: Think of a group decision that went badly. Was a two-party assumption — treating it as you versus one other person — part of why?

lessons.title: What You Don't Know About Them
objectives: Recognise information asymmetry in a negotiation and probe for it rather than assuming you already know the other side's position.
teach: You almost never know the other side's BATNA, reservation value, or true priorities for certain — you're negotiating with an estimate, built from what they say and do, not with their actual numbers.

Assuming you already know the other side's alternatives or constraints without having actually verified them. Confident guesses about someone else's position are still guesses, and treating them as facts can lead you to concede too much, or hold out for a deal that was never on the table.

Open, specific questions — not just watching for signals — are often the fastest way to narrow the gap between your estimate of the other side's position and the reality, though their answers still need weighing against what you independently know.
lessons.example: You assume a landlord won't budge on rent because the listing says 'firm.' Simply asking whether there's any flexibility, especially for a longer lease, sometimes reveals constraints — or lack of them — that the listing's wording never actually confirmed either way.
practicePrompts: Think of a negotiation where you assumed something about the other side's position.
Ask whether that assumption was ever actually confirmed, or just inferred.
Think of one specific question that could have tested it directly.
lessons.apply: In your next negotiation, ask at least one direct question aimed at testing an assumption you're making about the other side's constraints, rather than just acting on the assumption.
lessons.reflect: Where has an unverified assumption about someone else's position cost you in a past negotiation?

lessons.title: Why a 'Fair' Deal Sticks Better
objectives: Recognise that a deal perceived as unfair by the other side is less likely to be accepted or honoured, even if it benefits you numerically.
teach: People routinely reject or resent deals they see as unfair, even when the deal still leaves them better off than their alternative. A negotiation isn't just about the final number — it's also about whether the other side walks away feeling treated reasonably.

Optimising purely for your own numeric outcome while ignoring how the deal will be perceived. A technically 'winning' deal that the other side experiences as exploitative can fall apart, get renegotiated later, or damage a relationship you'll need again.

Framing matters here as much as substance: the same numeric outcome, explained with visible reasoning the other side can follow, tends to land as fairer than the identical outcome delivered as a flat take-it-or-leave-it.
lessons.example: A landlord raises rent exactly to what the market would bear, with no explanation. A tenant who feels blindsided may contest it, move out resentfully, or stop maintaining the place carefully — the same increase, explained with comparable listings shown upfront, is far more likely to be simply accepted.
practicePrompts: Think of a deal you negotiated that technically favoured you.
Consider how the other side likely experienced it — as fair, or as a loss.
Think of how you might have framed the same outcome to land better.
lessons.apply: In your next negotiation, explain your reasoning for an offer openly, not just the number itself, so the other side can see why it's reasonable.
lessons.reflect: Where has a deal that was good for you on paper caused problems later because the other side felt it was unfair?

lessons.title: Recognising When to Walk Away
objectives: Judge when an offer is actually worse than your reservation value, resisting both premature acceptance and ego-driven refusal.
teach: Walking away is the right call exactly when an offer is worse than your reservation value — not a moment before, and not a moment after. Both directions of error are common: accepting something worse than your BATNA out of fatigue or momentum, and refusing something better than your BATNA out of pride.

Treating 'walk away' as always the strong move, or always the weak one. Neither is true — the only question that actually matters is whether the specific offer on the table beats your specific reservation value, worked out before the pressure of the moment.

A clearly pre-set reservation value is what makes this judgment possible in the moment — without one, both over-accepting and over-refusing are easy to talk yourself into, because there's no fixed line to check the offer against.
lessons.example: You're negotiating a car's price and have a firm reservation value of $18,000, below your BATNA at another dealer. The seller's final offer is $18,200. Walking away over $200, on principle, is worse for you than accepting — just as accepting $19,500 out of exhaustion would also be a mistake, since it's worse than your own alternative.
practicePrompts: Think of a negotiation where you were tempted to accept out of fatigue.
Check whether the offer was actually above or below your reservation value.
Think of a case where pride, not the numbers, nearly made you walk away from a good deal.
lessons.apply: In your next negotiation, write your reservation value down before you start, and check any final offer against that exact number, not against how you feel in the moment.
lessons.reflect: Think back over this whole module. Which single idea — BATNA, ZOPA, anchoring, or walk-away judgment — do you most need to actually use next time you negotiate something real?

lessons.title: Complications
objectives: Combine multi-party dynamics, information asymmetry, fairness framing and walk-away judgment into reading a messier real negotiation.
teach: Real negotiations are rarely the clean two-party, full-information, single-round version the earlier weeks used to teach each idea cleanly. More parties, missing information, fairness concerns, and genuine uncertainty about when to walk away usually show up together, not one at a time.

Treating a complication as an excuse to abandon the preparation from weeks 5 and 6. A multi-party, uncertain, fairness-sensitive negotiation still benefits from knowing your BATNA and reservation value — the complications change the conversation, not the prep work underneath it.
This closes out the negotiation module. Everything from BATNA through walk-away judgment is meant to work together on one real negotiation, not as separate tools used one at a time.
lessons.example: Negotiating a shared family home's sale among three siblings involves all four complications at once: three parties with different financial needs (multiparty), uncertainty about what each sibling would actually accept (information asymmetry), a need for the split to feel fair to all three regardless of the legal minimum (fairness), and each sibling needing their own walk-away judgment about whether a buyout offer beats simply co-owning it longer.
practicePrompts: Think of a real negotiation involving more than two people or real uncertainty.
Identify which of this week's four complications are actually present in it.
Consider what preparation from weeks 5 and 6 still applies underneath the complications.
lessons.apply: Pick one real, upcoming negotiation in your life — even a small one — and prepare for it fully: BATNA, reservation value, likely ZOPA, interests behind positions, and which of this week's complications apply.
lessons.reflect: In your own words, describe a real negotiation you're facing or recently had: your BATNA and reservation value, where the ZOPA likely was, and which complications from this week applied.

concepts.label: A player is anyone whose choice affects the outcome
An action is one of the choices a player can make
Preferences rank the outcomes for one player, from the one they like most to the one they like least
A payoff is a number for how much a player likes an outcome
Timing says who chooses when: at the same time, or one after another
Information says what each player knows when choosing, including whether they have seen the other’s choice
There is strategic dependence when your result depends on someone else’s choice as well as your own
A best response is the action that gives you the highest payoff given the other player’s choice
In a coordination situation, your best response is to match the other’s choice; in an anti-coordination situation, to differ from it
When you are unsure what the other will do, a best response to your belief is the action with the highest average payoff, weighting each of their choices by how likely you think it is
A dominant strategy gives you a higher payoff than any other action, whatever the other player does
An action is dominated when another action gives you a higher payoff whatever the other player does
Iterated elimination removes dominated actions one round at a time, then checks again in what is left
An action weakly dominates another when it is never worse and sometimes better
A pair of choices where each is a best response to the other
A situation with more than one stable pair of choices
How repetition changes what's worth choosing
Starting cooperatively, then mirroring the other side's last choice
Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement
The actual point below which you walk away
The range where a deal is possible for both sides
What someone wants, versus what they're asking for
Splitting a fixed amount, versus growing what's available
How the first offer shapes the eventual outcome
What the size and pace of a concession reveals
Trading across issues valued differently by each side
How a third party changes a negotiation
What you don't know about the other side
Why a deal perceived as fair holds up better
Recognising when a deal is actually worse than your alternative

misconceptions.label: MODEL_EXTRA_PLAYER
misconceptions.description: Included someone who makes no choice that affects the outcome.

misconceptions.label: MODEL_MISSING_PLAYER
misconceptions.description: Left out someone whose choice affects the outcome.

misconceptions.label: MODEL_MISSING_ACTION
misconceptions.description: Left out an action a player can take.

misconceptions.label: MISREAD_PAYOFF_OWNER
misconceptions.description: Used the other player’s payoff as one’s own.

misconceptions.label: MODEL_WRONG_RANKING
misconceptions.description: Misordered a player’s preferences over outcomes.

misconceptions.label: MODEL_WRONG_INFO
misconceptions.description: Wrong account of who knows or sees what when choosing.

misconceptions.label: MODEL_WRONG_TIMING
misconceptions.description: Wrong order of choices.

misconceptions.label: IGNORED_DEPENDENCE
misconceptions.description: Treated one’s result as depending only on one’s own choice.

misconceptions.label: ACROSS_NOT_WITHIN
misconceptions.description: Compared cells across the other player’s actions instead of within one.

misconceptions.label: INCOMPLETE_COMPARISON
misconceptions.description: Compared payoffs for only one of the other player’s actions.

misconceptions.label: TREATING_TIE_AS_STRICT
misconceptions.description: Treated equal payoffs as though one action were strictly better.

misconceptions.label: NOT_BR_TO_OWN_PREDICTION
misconceptions.description: Chose an action that is not a best response to one’s own stated prediction or belief.

misconceptions.label: DOMINANCE_FROM_OUTCOME
misconceptions.description: Called an action better whatever happens because it led to a good outcome once.

misconceptions.label: IGNORED_OPPONENT_INCENTIVE
misconceptions.description: Expected the other player to pick an action that is worse for them whatever happens.

misconceptions.label: INDIVIDUAL_AS_JOINT
misconceptions.description: Assumed that choices each better for their owner give an outcome no other outcome improves on for both.

misconceptions.label: ELIMINATED_UNDOMINATED
misconceptions.description: Set aside an action that is not worse in every case.

misconceptions.label: WEAK_AS_STRICT
misconceptions.description: Called a weakly dominant action strictly dominant: treated a tie as a win when comparing across all of the other’s choices.

misconceptions.label: Equilibrium mistaken for the best outcome
misconceptions.description: Treating a stable pair of choices as the best possible result for both players, rather than simply one neither side wants to unilaterally change.

misconceptions.label: Ignored a second stable pair
misconceptions.description: Checking only one pair of choices for stability and missing that a different pair is also stable.

misconceptions.label: One-shot reasoning applied to a repeated situation
misconceptions.description: Reasoning about a choice as if this were the only round, ignoring how it will shape the other player's choices in future rounds.

misconceptions.label: Reciprocity mistaken for unconditional cooperation
misconceptions.description: Treating a reciprocal strategy as always cooperating regardless of what the other side does, rather than mirroring their last choice.

misconceptions.label: BATNA ignored
misconceptions.description: Negotiating without working out your best alternative to a deal, so there's no way to tell a good offer from a bad one.

misconceptions.label: Reservation value confused with target
misconceptions.description: Treating your walk-away point (reservation value) as the same thing as your hoped-for outcome (target), when they're different numbers serving different purposes.

misconceptions.label: ZOPA assumed without checking
misconceptions.description: Assuming a deal is possible without checking whether the two sides' acceptable ranges actually overlap.

misconceptions.label: Position mistaken for interest
misconceptions.description: Treating what someone is asking for (their position) as the same thing as what they actually want (their interest), missing room for a different solution that serves the same want.

misconceptions.label: Negotiation assumed purely distributive
misconceptions.description: Treating every negotiation as a fixed pie to be split, missing opportunities to create additional value both sides could share.

misconceptions.label: Passively letting the other side anchor
misconceptions.description: Defaulting to let the other party make the first offer without considering that doing so often shifts the eventual outcome in their favour.

misconceptions.label: Concession pattern misread
misconceptions.description: Reading a concession's size or speed as revealing something it doesn't — for instance, assuming a quick concession always signals weakness rather than a low-priority issue.

misconceptions.label: Single-issue framing
misconceptions.description: Negotiating one issue at a time instead of bundling several, missing trades that would let each side get more of what they value most.

misconceptions.label: Two-party assumption in a multi-party situation
misconceptions.description: Reasoning as if only two parties are involved when a third party's presence, alliances, or sequencing actually changes the dynamics.

misconceptions.label: Overconfidence about the other side's BATNA
misconceptions.description: Assuming you know the other party's alternatives or walk-away point without having actually verified it.

misconceptions.label: Fairness perception ignored
misconceptions.description: Focusing only on your own numeric outcome while ignoring whether the other side will see the deal as fair enough to actually accept or honour.

misconceptions.label: Walk-away point misjudged
misconceptions.description: Either accepting a deal worse than your reservation value out of momentum, or walking away from a deal that actually beat it, out of ego or overconfidence.
